case_info.scenario: A woman in her mid-70s with a medical history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and left anterior descending artery stenting complained of unexplained dyspnea on exertion. An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

case_info.explanation: Rate-related LBBB resulting in acute severe MR B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing The patient’s paroxysmal symptoms were attributed to rate-related LBBB, which resulted in acute dyssynchrony of LV contraction and severe MR with symptoms of dyspnea. In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. The probability of success of LBBP was high due to the direct correlation between the severe MR and LBBB, as determined by exercise TTE and the immediate reduction of MR upon return to narrow QRS complexes. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. The initiation of β-blockers as a rate-control therapy with the objective of avoiding the reappearance of LBBB (and therefore MR) represents a potential alternative. However, this therapy is unlikely to provide sufficient relief from symptoms, given that the heart rate threshold for LBBB recurrence was relatively low in this patient, at approximately 75 beats per minute (bpm). Conventional CRT with BVP was first attempted but was unsuccessful due to lack of suitable coronary vein. LBBP was performed as an alternative, achieving successful physiological pacing (Figure 2). At the 3-week follow-up appointment, the patient reported a significant improvement in her quality of life, with the absence of any further episodes of dyspnea. An exercise TTE performed until a heart rate of 120 bpm was reached demonstrated no widening of QRS complexes and mild MR that did not worsen with exercise (Video).

case_info.caption: Transthoracic echocardiogram with apical 4-chamber views showing severe mitral regurgitation at a heart rate of 95 beats per minute (bpm), with wide QRS on monitoring (A), and minimal mitral regurgitation at a resting heart rate of 58 bpm, with narrow QRS on monitoring (B).
case_info.explanation: Rate-related LBBB resulting in acute severe MR B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing The patient’s paroxysmal symptoms were attributed to rate-related LBBB, which resulted in acute dyssynchrony of LV contraction and severe MR with symptoms of dyspnea. In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. The probability of success of LBBP was high due to the direct correlation between the severe MR and LBBB, as determined by exercise TTE and the immediate reduction of MR upon return to narrow QRS complexes. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. The initiation of β-blockers as a rate-control therapy with the objective of avoiding the reappearance of LBBB (and therefore MR) represents a potential alternative. However, this therapy is unlikely to provide sufficient relief from symptoms, given that the heart rate threshold for LBBB recurrence was relatively low in this patient, at approximately 75 beats per minute (bpm). Conventional CRT with BVP was first attempted but was unsuccessful due to lack of suitable coronary vein. LBBP was performed as an alternative, achieving successful physiological pacing (Figure 2). At the 3-week follow-up appointment, the patient reported a significant improvement in her quality of life, with the absence of any further episodes of dyspnea. An exercise TTE performed until a heart rate of 120 bpm was reached demonstrated no widening of QRS complexes and mild MR that did not worsen with exercise (Video).

Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing The patient’s paroxysmal symptoms were attributed to rate-related LBBB, which resulted in acute dyssynchrony of LV contraction and severe MR with symptoms of dyspnea. In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. The probability of success of LBBP was high due to the direct correlation between the severe MR and LBBB, as determined by exercise TTE and the immediate reduction of MR upon return to narrow QRS complexes. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. The initiation of β-blockers as a rate-control therapy with the objective of avoiding the reappearance of LBBB (and therefore MR) represents a potential alternative. However, this therapy is unlikely to provide sufficient relief from symptoms, given that the heart rate threshold for LBBB recurrence was relatively low in this patient, at approximately 75 beats per minute (bpm). Conventional CRT with BVP was first attempted but was unsuccessful due to lack of suitable coronary vein. LBBP was performed as an alternative, achieving successful physiological pacing (Figure 2). At the 3-week follow-up appointment, the patient reported a significant improvement in her quality of life, with the absence of any further episodes of dyspnea. case_info.explanation: Rate-related LBBB resulting in acute severe MR B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing The patient’s paroxysmal symptoms were attributed to rate-related LBBB, which resulted in acute dyssynchrony of LV contraction and severe MR with symptoms of dyspnea. In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. The probability of success of LBBP was high due to the direct correlation between the severe MR and LBBB, as determined by exercise TTE and the immediate reduction of MR upon return to narrow QRS complexes. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. The initiation of β-blockers as a rate-control therapy with the objective of avoiding the reappearance of LBBB (and therefore MR) represents a potential alternative. However, this therapy is unlikely to provide sufficient relief from symptoms, given that the heart rate threshold for LBBB recurrence was relatively low in this patient, at approximately 75 beats per minute (bpm). Conventional CRT with BVP was first attempted but was unsuccessful due to lack of suitable coronary vein. LBBP was performed as an alternative, achieving successful physiological pacing (Figure 2). At the 3-week follow-up appointment, the patient reported a significant improvement in her quality of life, with the absence of any further episodes of dyspnea. An exercise TTE performed until a heart rate of 120 bpm was reached demonstrated no widening of QRS complexes and mild MR that did not worsen with exercise (Video).

case_info.caption: Transthoracic echocardiogram with apical 4-chamber views showing severe mitral regurgitation at a heart rate of 95 beats per minute (bpm), with wide QRS on monitoring (A), and minimal mitral regurgitation at a resting heart rate of 58 bpm, with narrow QRS on monitoring (B).
case_info.explanation: Rate-related LBBB resulting in acute severe MR B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing The patient’s paroxysmal symptoms were attributed to rate-related LBBB, which resulted in acute dyssynchrony of LV contraction and severe MR with symptoms of dyspnea. In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. The probability of success of LBBP was high due to the direct correlation between the severe MR and LBBB, as determined by exercise TTE and the immediate reduction of MR upon return to narrow QRS complexes. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. The initiation of β-blockers as a rate-control therapy with the objective of avoiding the reappearance of LBBB (and therefore MR) represents a potential alternative. However, this therapy is unlikely to provide sufficient relief from symptoms, given that the heart rate threshold for LBBB recurrence was relatively low in this patient, at approximately 75 beats per minute (bpm). Conventional CRT with BVP was first attempted but was unsuccessful due to lack of suitable coronary vein. LBBP was performed as an alternative, achieving successful physiological pacing (Figure 2). At the 3-week follow-up appointment, the patient reported a significant improvement in her quality of life, with the absence of any further episodes of dyspnea. An exercise TTE performed until a heart rate of 120 bpm was reached demonstrated no widening of QRS complexes and mild MR that did not worsen with exercise (Video).

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."

   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

case_info.caption: Transthoracic echocardiogram with apical 4-chamber views showing severe mitral regurgitation at a heart rate of 95 beats per minute (bpm), with wide QRS on monitoring (A), and minimal mitral regurgitation at a resting heart rate of 58 bpm, with narrow QRS on monitoring (B).
case_info.explanation: Rate-related LBBB resulting in acute severe MR B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing The patient’s paroxysmal symptoms were attributed to rate-related LBBB, which resulted in acute dyssynchrony of LV contraction and severe MR with symptoms of dyspnea. In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. The probability of success of LBBP was high due to the direct correlation between the severe MR and LBBB, as determined by exercise TTE and the immediate reduction of MR upon return to narrow QRS complexes. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. The initiation of β-blockers as a rate-control therapy with the objective of avoiding the reappearance of LBBB (and therefore MR) represents a potential alternative. However, this therapy is unlikely to provide sufficient relief from symptoms, given that the heart rate threshold for LBBB recurrence was relatively low in this patient, at approximately 75 beats per minute (bpm). Conventional CRT with BVP was first attempted but was unsuccessful due to lack of suitable coronary vein. LBBP was performed as an alternative, achieving successful physiological pacing (Figure 2). At the 3-week follow-up appointment, the patient reported a significant improvement in her quality of life, with the absence of any further episodes of dyspnea. An exercise TTE performed until a heart rate of 120 bpm was reached demonstrated no widening of QRS complexes and mild MR that did not worsen with exercise (Video).

   Definition:

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

case_info.explanation: Rate-related LBBB resulting in acute severe MR B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing The patient’s paroxysmal symptoms were attributed to rate-related LBBB, which resulted in acute dyssynchrony of LV contraction and severe MR with symptoms of dyspnea. In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. The probability of success of LBBP was high due to the direct correlation between the severe MR and LBBB, as determined by exercise TTE and the immediate reduction of MR upon return to narrow QRS complexes. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. The initiation of β-blockers as a rate-control therapy with the objective of avoiding the reappearance of LBBB (and therefore MR) represents a potential alternative. However, this therapy is unlikely to provide sufficient relief from symptoms, given that the heart rate threshold for LBBB recurrence was relatively low in this patient, at approximately 75 beats per minute (bpm). Conventional CRT with BVP was first attempted but was unsuccessful due to lack of suitable coronary vein. LBBP was performed as an alternative, achieving successful physiological pacing (Figure 2). At the 3-week follow-up appointment, the patient reported a significant improvement in her quality of life, with the absence of any further episodes of dyspnea. An exercise TTE performed until a heart rate of 120 bpm was reached demonstrated no widening of QRS complexes and mild MR that did not worsen with exercise (Video).

You are a deliberation POLICY steering a conversation between a medical AI and a clinician toward
the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when

case_info.scenario: A woman in her mid-70s with a medical history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and left anterior descending artery stenting complained of unexplained dyspnea on exertion. An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

case_info.caption: Transthoracic echocardiogram with apical 4-chamber views showing severe mitral regurgitation at a heart rate of 95 beats per minute (bpm), with wide QRS on monitoring (A), and minimal mitral regurgitation at a resting heart rate of 58 bpm, with narrow QRS on monitoring (B).
case_info.explanation: Rate-related LBBB resulting in acute severe MR B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing The patient’s paroxysmal symptoms were attributed to rate-related LBBB, which resulted in acute dyssynchrony of LV contraction and severe MR with symptoms of dyspnea. In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. The probability of success of LBBP was high due to the direct correlation between the severe MR and LBBB, as determined by exercise TTE and the immediate reduction of MR upon return to narrow QRS complexes. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. The initiation of β-blockers as a rate-control therapy with the objective of avoiding the reappearance of LBBB (and therefore MR) represents a potential alternative. However, this therapy is unlikely to provide sufficient relief from symptoms, given that the heart rate threshold for LBBB recurrence was relatively low in this patient, at approximately 75 beats per minute (bpm). Conventional CRT with BVP was first attempted but was unsuccessful due to lack of suitable coronary vein. LBBP was performed as an alternative, achieving successful physiological pacing (Figure 2). At the 3-week follow-up appointment, the patient reported a significant improvement in her quality of life, with the absence of any further episodes of dyspnea. An exercise TTE performed until a heart rate of 120 bpm was reached demonstrated no widening of QRS complexes and mild MR that did not worsen with exercise (Video).

An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.
